name: Sebadoh
label: Sub Pop
lede: Lou Barlow got pushed out of Dinosaur Jr., wrote a song about it, and with Eric Gaffney and Jason Loewenstein turned four-track tapes and three clashing songwriters into the sound of '90s indie rock.

eras.title: The songs Dinosaur Jr. didn't need
eras.text: While J Mascis took over Dinosaur Jr., its bassist Lou Barlow was filling cassettes at home in western Massachusetts. With Eric Gaffney he turned that habit into a band, and when Dinosaur Jr. threw him out, Sebadoh became his whole life.

years.h: Lou Barlow and Eric Gaffney start Sebadoh in Northampton
years.p: [[Lou Barlow|6523f86d-11d3-489e-81f6-6cbe08c367de]] was playing bass in [[Dinosaur Jr.|77c167d2-4965-4421-830a-9815e4956475]], where [[J Mascis|82315599-2215-4c3e-a36f-87be58d06ec0]] had taken creative control. Sebadoh, with [[Eric Gaffney|820d149f-836a-4527-a2ab-14fb079bc212]], was his outlet.

years.h: The Weed Forestin' cassette, named for a Barlow mumble
years.p: Sebadoh's first tape. The band name was a nonsense word Lou Barlow kept muttering on his home recordings.

years.h: Lou Barlow is kicked out of Dinosaur Jr.
years.p: After the band's third album, Bug, and years of friction with J Mascis, Barlow is out. From here Sebadoh is his main band.

years.h: The Freed Man: Gerard Cosloy puts the tapes on Homestead
years.p: Homestead boss [[Gerard Cosloy|b3c600d5-e1dd-4525-855d-6d4f950c3be6]] issues Sebadoh's home recordings as a full LP, Barlow and Gaffney songs side by side.

years.h: Jason Loewenstein joins Sebadoh
years.p: [[Jason Loewenstein|d06bfcfa-7be5-40ca-82be-4c7d3bdb44c3]] makes it a trio. Across 1989 and 1990 the band plays only about ten shows, in western Massachusetts, Boston and New York.

eras.title: Four tracks and a song for J Mascis
eras.text: Three songwriters who pulled in different directions: Barlow's bruised folk, Gaffney's drones and hardcore bursts, Loewenstein somewhere between. Cheap records made them the face of a genre people started calling lo-fi.

years.h: Gimme Indie Rock, the first single with Jason Loewenstein
years.p: Sebadoh's Homestead single sends up the scene it's part of, and becomes one of its anthems.

years.h: Sebadoh III: $1,300 and a genre called lo-fi
years.p: Made in late March 1991 at Fort Apache in Boston and at home. Spin put it at No. 41 of the '90s; it sits next to Pavement's Slanted and Enchanted as a lo-fi cornerstone.

years.h: "The Freed Pig": Lou Barlow opens Sebadoh III at J Mascis
years.p: The first track on Sebadoh III is Lou Barlow's answer to being thrown out of Dinosaur Jr. [[The Breeders|667e856e-f3a7-42e9-8244-95422ef31321]] covered The Freed Pig in 1994.

years.h: A tour with fIREHOSE, then a deal with Sub Pop
years.p: After the road with [[Mike Watt|568203ae-c27b-4990-8997-09c0d5c0de77]]'s [[fIREHOSE|33e09dd8-a998-4e1a-9e69-1a6567a3803d]], Sebadoh signs to Sub Pop in the US, Domino in the UK and City Slang in Germany.

years.h: Two EPs become Smash Your Head on the Punk Rock
years.p: Sub Pop combines the Rocking the Forest and Sebadoh vs. Helmet EPs, released two months apart, into one American album.
years.xp: Eric Gaffney kept leaving and coming back, three times between 1990 and 1993. His fill-in, Boston record-store clerk [[Bob Fay|87509777-a7ba-4a80-aa83-42dc8819236e]], plays on half of Rocking the Forest and two tracks of Sebadoh vs. Helmet.

eras.title: Gaffney walks, Bakesale lands
eras.text: Sebadoh moved into real studios and Eric Gaffney moved out. With Bob Fay behind the kit and Jason Loewenstein now an equal writer, the band made its most loved record.

years.h: Bubble & Scrape: the first all-studio Sebadoh album
years.p: Engineered by [[Bob Weston|7364260a-0a3e-4a6c-bcf8-b4e743c0b2c0]], and the last with Eric Gaffney songs. Lou Barlow sings a duet with Seana Carmody of [[Swirlies|4ec4a033-ba44-41ca-8e09-3bf94fc08523]].

years.h: Eric Gaffney quits Sebadoh in the middle of Bakesale
years.p: Gaffney wanted a third of the advance, his own sessions and no touring. Lou Barlow said no, and Bob Fay took over the drums.
years.xp:
Barlow told Under the Radar that Gaffney had already bailed on Sebadoh's first tour with [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] a week earlier. Gaffney's own account: he felt like it, and wanted a band where he was the songwriter and guitarist.

Loewenstein went from one or two songs a record to an equal partner.

years.h: Bakesale: Lou Barlow, age one, on the cover
years.p: Barlow's mother took the cover photo; Bob Fay and his brothers are on the back. It reached No. 40 in the UK and No. 16 on Spin's best of 1994.
years.xp: Sessions ran at Steve Albini's Chicago home with engineer Bob Weston, and at Fort Apache in Boston, with Tim O'Heir producing. Barlow borrowed John Davis's vintage amps from their Folk Implosion sessions.

years.h: Lou Barlow's side band has a hit: Natural One
years.p: [[The Folk Implosion|31722656-e14d-4f3f-8ecb-27cba9ce3a15]], Barlow's duo with John Davis, goes Top 40 with Natural One from the Kids soundtrack.

eras.title: Fire your drummer
eras.text: Success brought money and outside advice. Sebadoh charted, fired Bob Fay, signed to a major, made an expensive record in Los Angeles while Lou Barlow's life came apart, and then just stopped.

q: You've got to fire your drummer.
a Harmacy producer, as Lou Barlow recalls
years.h: Sub Pop spends big on Harmacy and the producer wants Bob Fay gone
years.p: Lou Barlow says the pressure started right away: the drumming wasn't good enough. Bob Fay played on Harmacy anyway, his last Sebadoh album.

years.h: Harmacy: a pharmacy in Cashel, Ireland, missing its P
years.p: Jason Loewenstein shot the cover on tour. Sebadoh's first charting US album, No. 126, with Ocean at No. 23 on Modern Rock.

years.h: Bob Fay is fired; Louisville's Russ Pollard takes over
years.p: Jason Loewenstein brings in his friend [[Russ Pollard|986b1847-ebee-47e5-92a6-cdd864f3b287]], who can also switch instruments. Sebadoh signs to Sire while still owing Sub Pop.
years.xp: Per Vice, the major-label advances for Sebadoh on Sire and the Folk Implosion on Interscope helped pay for Lou Barlow's house in Silver Lake.

years.h: Five weeks at Chick Corea's studio for The Sebadoh
years.p: Sebadoh made The Sebadoh at Mad Hatter in Los Angeles. Jason Loewenstein remembers the luxury: two days to get one song right.
years.xp: Lou Barlow told Vice it was his worst year: he'd found out his wife was having an affair and was using speed during the sessions. He says he was trying not to fall apart between vocal takes on Tree.

years.h: The Sebadoh: No. 197 for one week, then Sire drops them
years.p: Flame reached No. 30 in the UK, but the album sold about a quarter of Harmacy's first-year total. Sire let the band go within weeks.

years.h: Twenty people in Dallas on a Modest Mouse tour
years.p: Sebadoh had drawn 400 or 500 in Dallas before. On tour with [[Modest Mouse|a96ac800-bfcb-412a-8a63-0a98df600700]], Lou Barlow says the indifference was palpable.

years.h: Sebadoh goes on hiatus
years.p: Lou Barlow turns to the Folk Implosion; Jason Loewenstein works on his solo album At Sixes and Sevens. Barlow says he just gave up, and they barely spoke for two or three years.

eras.title: Domino's party and the classic three
eras.text: A record label's birthday brought the band back, first as a duo. Four years later the original trio, Eric Gaffney included, was on the road for the first time in fourteen years.

years.h: Domino's 10th anniversary brings Sebadoh back as a duo
years.p: Domino Records asks Sebadoh to play its birthday. Lou Barlow and Jason Loewenstein reform and play shows into early 2004.

years.h: Lou Barlow rejoins Dinosaur Jr.
years.p: The original Dinosaur Jr. lineup, Barlow and J Mascis included, reunites on The Late Late Show with Craig Ferguson.

years.h: The Sebadoh III trio tours again, first time in 14 years
years.p: Billed as Sebadoh Classic, the Sebadoh III lineup hits the road as Domino begins reissuing the early albums.

years.h: Bubble & Scrape in full at Koko, London
years.p: Sebadoh plays the album front to back for All Tomorrow's Parties' Don't Look Back series.

eras.title: Post-drama
eras.text: With Bob D'Amico on drums, Sebadoh became a working band again: reissues, two albums on indie labels, and none of the chaos. Barlow's word for it is post-drama.

years.h: Bob D'Amico replaces Eric Gaffney on drums
years.p: [[Bob D'Amico|7d469750-76ea-43ea-aa43-c0566c5fa4d2]], Jason Loewenstein's bandmate in [[The Fiery Furnaces|2c916f95-f6ba-46fa-b9d8-dc0d9379f603]] and Circle of Buzzards, joins for a tour behind the Bakesale deluxe reissue.

years.h: Jeff Mangum picks Sebadoh for All Tomorrow's Parties
years.p: [[Neutral Milk Hotel|a506f761-2c22-4b2f-8a94-bd748c2c8f75]]'s [[Jeff Mangum|6a7b9d5e-a863-4a90-a056-77942e9f43de]] invites Sebadoh to his ATP in Minehead, the same month Weed Forestin' is reissued.

years.h: Defend Yourself: the first Sebadoh album in 14 years
years.p: Out on Joyful Noise, it debuted at No. 1 on a Billboard chart for new alternative artists, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Act Surprised on Dangerbird
years.p: Sebadoh's ninth album, made with Bob D'Amico. Lou Barlow says there's no drama anymore.

years.h: Harmacy at 30: a Sub Pop expanded edition
years.p: Due on double LP and CD with 16 bonus tracks: alternate versions, B-sides, BBC sessions and live cuts.

sources.title: Under the Radar: Lou Barlow on the 20th Anniversary of Bakesale
